qs.q: During an anatomical dissection of the interscalene triangle, a student identifies the boundaries. Which of the following correctly describes the boundaries of this primary thoracic outlet passageway?
o: Coracoid process, pectoralis minor tendon, and second rib
Middle third of the clavicle, first rib, and upper scapula
Anterior scalene muscle, middle scalene, and first rib surface
Anterior scalene muscle, clavicle, and subclavian vein
qs.e: The interscalene triangle is bordered anteriorly by the anterior scalene muscle, posteriorly by the middle scalene muscle, and inferiorly by the medial surface of the first rib. The costoclavicular space is bounded by the clavicle, first rib, and scapula.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: Which provocative examination test is widely considered the most useful screening test for all three types of thoracic outlet syndrome because it challenges all three anatomical passageways?
o: Wright's hyperabduction manoeuvre testing vascular flow
Elevated arm stress test (EAST or Roos test)
Adson's test with neck extension and head rotation
Costoclavicular military brace manoeuvre assessment
qs.e: The elevated arm stress test (EAST or Roos test) involves opening and closing the hands for 3 minutes with arms abducted and is the most useful screening test for all three types. Adson's test specifically targets subclavian artery compression rather than screening all types.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: A young, thin female patient with drooping shoulders exhibits true neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome characterized by the classic Gilliatt-Sumner hand. Which intrinsic hand muscle experiences the most pronounced wasting in this specific presentation?
o: The abductor digiti minimi intrinsic hand muscle
The abductor pollicis brevis intrinsic hand muscle
The first dorsal interosseous intrinsic hand muscle
The first lumbrical intrinsic hand muscle
qs.e: True neurogenic TOS classically features the Gilliatt-Sumner hand, which shows prominent wasting of the abductor pollicis brevis with lesser involvement of the interossei and hypothenar muscles. Interossei wasting is more characteristic of ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome without objective neurological deficits or a bony anomaly. What is the most appropriate initial management plan?
o: Immediate surgical scalenectomy and brachial exploration
Physiotherapy for 3 to 6 months including posture correction
Urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis and venous stenting
Immediate transaxillary first rib resection and neurolysis
qs.e: Neurogenic TOS without objective deficits or bony anomalies is initially managed with conservative physiotherapy. Surgery is reserved for cases refractory to conservative care or those with significant neurological loss.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: When performing Adson's test during the evaluation of a patient suspected of having thoracic outlet syndrome, what specific physical action is performed by the patient to elicit the sign?
o: Takes a deep breath, extends neck, turns head to side
Retracts and depresses shoulders in military attention
Abducts both shoulders with elbows flexed and hands
Passively hyperabducts the arm above head for bruits
qs.e: Adson's test requires the patient to take a deep breath, extend the neck, and turn the head to the affected side to evaluate for the loss of the radial pulse. The hand-opening maneuver describes the Roos test rather than Adson's test.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: A 35-year-old male presents with signs of arterial thoracic outlet syndrome. Which clinical finding is a particularly reliable indicator of arterial involvement rather than neurogenic or venous disease?
o: Isolated wasting of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle
Nocturnal paraesthesia in the ring and little fingers
Sudden arm cyanosis and distended chest wall veins
A blood pressure difference of over 20 mmHg in arms
qs.e: A blood pressure difference of over 20 mmHg between arms is a reliable indicator of arterial TOS due to subclavian artery stenosis or compression. Cyanosis and distended chest wall veins are classic features of venous thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter syndrome).
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: What is the reported relative frequency of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome compared to venous and arterial forms?
o: About 95% of all reported clinical cases
About 15% of all reported clinical cases
About 75% of all reported clinical cases
About 50% of all reported clinical cases
qs.e: Neurogenic TOS accounts for about 95% of cases, while venous TOS accounts for 4% and arterial TOS accounts for 1%. It is by far the most common presentation among the three forms.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following congenital skeletal anomalies is well-documented to narrow the thoracic outlet spaces and contribute to compression syndromes?
o: A congenital lumbarized sacral skeletal segment
A congenital bifid xiphoid skeletal process
An accessory tenth rib skeletal structure
A congenital cervical rib skeletal anomaly
qs.e: A cervical rib (found in 0.5 to 1% of people) is a well-known anomaly that narrows the thoracic outlet passageways. Bifid xiphoid processes have no anatomical relationship to the superior thoracic aperture.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

es.q: List and explain the three anatomical passageways involved in thoracic outlet syndrome and the structures they contain.
es.m:
- **The interscalene triangle:** Bordered by the anterior scalene muscle anteriorly, middle scalene muscle posteriorly, and medial surface of the first rib inferiorly; transmits the brachial plexus trunks and the subclavian artery.
- **The costoclavicular triangle:** Located between the middle third of the clavicle anteriorly, the first rib posteromedially, and the upper border of the scapula posterolaterally; contains the brachial plexus, subclavian artery, and subclavian vein.
- **The subcoracoid space:** Situated beneath the coracoid process and deep to the pectoralis minor tendon.
- **Significance:** These three passageways are narrowed by congenital anomalies, fibrous bands, or trauma,
es.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: Essay questions

es.q: Outline the clinical features and examination findings characteristic of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome.
es.m:
- **Lower roots involvement (C8, T1 in ~90%):** Causes pain and paraesthesia in the ulnar nerve distribution, often nocturnal and triggered by overhead activity.
- **Functional deficits:** Loss of dexterity, weakness of grip, and cold intolerance (Raynaud-like picture), plus neck pain and headache.
- **True neurogenic TOS phenotype:** Classic presentation in a young, thin woman with a long neck and drooping shoulders.
- **Specific signs:** Supraclavicular tenderness, subtle weakness, and the Gilliatt-Sumner hand (wasting of the abductor pollicis brevis predominantly).
- **Upper roots involvement (C5-C7):** Less common; causes pain in the neck, ear, upper chest, back, and outer arm.
es.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: Essay questions

es.q: Discuss the classification, anatomical background, clinical presentation, diagnostic investigations, and management strategies for Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS).
es.m:
- **Background and definition:** Compression of neurovascular structures at the superior aperture of the thorax; symptoms, cause, diagnosis, and treatment are controversial.
- **Subtypes and epidemiology:** Brachial plexus affected in 95% (neurogenic TOS), subclavian vein in 4% (venous TOS, Paget-Schroetter), and subclavian artery in 1% (arterial TOS); overall 3 times commoner in women, with onset at 20 to 50 years.
- **Anatomical passageways:** Three key passageways subject to narrowing are the interscalene triangle, the costoclavicular triangle, and the subcoracoid space.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The thoracic outlet is the space between the neck and axilla through which neurovascular structures pass to the upper limb. Compression here causes neurogenic, venous or arterial symptoms. Understanding its borders helps diagnose thoracic outlet syndrome.

sections.p: The thoracic outlet (inlet) is the anatomical corridor linking the cervical region to the axilla. It contains the subclavian vessels and the brachial plexus trunks.
b: Key for upper‑limb blood flow and nerve function

sections.p: Boundaries: anterior – posterior border of the sternum to the xiphisternal joint; posterior – anterior surface of T1‑T12 vertebral bodies; lateral – first rib and its costal cartilage; inferior – the diaphragm.
The subclavian artery and vein run over the first rib, while the brachial plexus trunks pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles.
b: Cervical rib (if present) narrows the space
Fibrous bands or hypertrophic scalene muscles further reduce clearance

sections.p: Subclavian artery (continuation of the aortic arch on the left, brachiocephalic trunk on the right) supplies the upper limb; the subclavian vein returns blood.
b: Arterial compression can cause ischemic hand symptoms
Venous compression leads to swelling and collateral veins

sections.p: The brachial plexus trunks (C5‑T1) traverse the outlet, providing motor and sensory innervation to the arm.
b: Compression produces numbness, tingling, or weakness in the hand

sections.p: Provides a protected passage for neurovascular bundles while allowing shoulder and neck movement. Proper spacing prevents traction or compression during arm elevation.
b: Maintains perfusion and sensation of the upper limb
Allows full range of motion of the shoulder girdle

sections.p: Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) results from compression of neurovascular structures. It may be neurogenic (most common), venous, or arterial. Causes include congenital cervical rib, trauma, repetitive overhead activity, and hypertrophic scalene muscles. In low‑resource settings, infections (TB lymphadenitis) or scar tissue from herbal poultices can also narrow the outlet.
b: Neurogenic TOS: paresthesia, weakness, aggravated by arm elevation
Venous TOS: arm swelling, superficial collateral veins
Arterial TOS: coldness, pallor, possible embolic events

sections.p: Provocative maneuvers (Adson, Roos, Wright) reproduce symptoms by narrowing the outlet. Look for cervical rib on X‑ray, and assess for vascular compromise with pulse changes.

t.b: Does the patient develop dizziness or loss of radial pulse on neck extension and head rotation? Positive suggests neurovascular compression.
Is there flow reduction in the subclavian artery/vein with arm abduction? Confirms functional compression.
Is a cervical rib or abnormal first rib present? Identifies an anatomic cause.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of hand pulse or color suggesting arterial embolism
Rapid arm swelling with venous distension indicating thrombosis
Severe neurological deficit (weakness, loss of sensation) after trauma

faq.q: Why does raising the arm worsen symptoms?
faq.a: Arm elevation narrows the space between the scalene muscles and first rib, increasing compression on nerves or vessels.

faq.q: Can TOS be caused by infection?
faq.a: Yes, tuberculous lymphadenitis or chronic abscesses in the neck can compress the outlet, especially in low‑resource settings.

faq.q: Is a cervical rib always symptomatic?
faq.a: No, many people have an asymptomatic cervical rib; symptoms appear only when additional factors further reduce the outlet size.
